title: French AgTech startup Tellia raises €4.3 million to scale voice-enabled data capture
content: Tellia, the Paris-based voice AI assistant for agriculture founded in 2024, has raised a €4.3 million ($5 million) pre-Seed to scale technology that lets.
raw_content: Tellia, the Paris-based voice AI assistant for agriculture founded in 2024, has raised a €4.3 million ($5 million) pre-Seed to scale technology that lets farmers, agronomists and field teams capture and use their data simply by speaking. The pre-Seed round was led by Revent, with participation from Grey Silo Ventures (CVC of Cereal Docks Group), Jeriko (operated by Techmind) and Fund F. “The Ag industry keeps facing the same challenge: the people who spend their days in the field spend their evenings at a keyboard.” said Coline Labadie de Faÿ, CEO and co-founder of Tellia. “That was never a data problem. It was an interface problem. Traditional software cannot accept it the way it actually comes out, spoken, in the field, in whatever language the team works in. “So we did not build another platform that wants to own all the data. Instead, we built the interface. You talk, Tellia captures it, structures it, and interprets it into something the whole operation can act on. This funding round lets us push the voice AI further, build the agentic layer that sits between the field and the rest of the AgTech stack, and grow our team in the US and Europe.” Tellia’s raise comes amid continued investment in AI and technology-enabled agriculture across Europe in 2026. Among the largest comparable rounds covered by EU-Startups, Belgium’s Rainbow Crops raised €9.7 million to advance its AI-supported crop gene-editing platform, while London-based Biographica secured €8 million to develop its AI platform for climate-resilient crop varieties. In France, UBEES also raised €8 million to expand its technology-enabled regenerative agriculture operations and connected-hive monitoring capabilities. Together, these three rounds account for €25.7 million in disclosed funding; while including Tellia’s financing brings and other comparable disclosed rounds covered by EU-Startups, brings that total to approximately €42.2 million. Because no two operations work the same way, Tellia says it shapes its structure around how each farm actually runs, instead of forcing teams into a fixed template. The result is an agricultural agent that is easier to use than traditional software, more complete and more valuable in the field. Tellia says the funding will accelerate the rollout of their agentic AI suite. Partners embed it through a simple API: their users just talk, and Tellia captures, structures and interprets the field, delivering records and recommendations directly inside the partner’s own product. This is said to give richer data and higher daily usage.

title: Tellia raises $5 million to give farmers a voice in the field
content: The pre-seed round, led by Revent, comes as Tellia scales live deployments across the US and Europe. Tellia's voice AI turns everyday calls, texts and voice...
raw_content: - The pre-seed round, led by Revent, comes as Tellia scales live deployments across the US and Europe. - Tellia’s voice AI turns everyday calls, texts and voice notes from farm teams into structured field data. San Francisco & Paris, 8th September 2026 – Tellia, the voice AI assistant for agriculture, has raised $5 million to scale technology that lets farmers, agronomists and field teams capture and use their data simply by speaking. The pre-seed round was led by Revent, with participation from Grey Silo Ventures (CVC of Cereal Docks Group), Jeriko (operated by Techmind) and Fund F. Despite the growing volume of software built for agriculture, much of it still relies on screens, forms and manual data entry, with interfaces designed for the office rather than the field. Critical information from day-to-day operations, from disease sightings and spray decisions to scouting notes and crew updates, is still often captured in notebooks, messaging threads or memory instead of the systems designed to support action. Tellia reinvents this interface with a voice AI layer that lets users capture information in natural language through phone calls, voice notes, text, WhatsApp or email. It turns those inputs into clean, structured records connected to the right field, crop, crew and operation, while enabling users to ask questions and receive instant operational or agronomic answers. Because no two operations work the same way, Tellia shapes its structure around how each farm actually runs, instead of forcing teams into a fixed template. The result is an agricultural agent that is easier to use than traditional software, more complete and more valuable in the field. The company has built strong early commercial traction; in the US, where the product first launched, Tellia reaches 80% daily active usage among field teams within two months of onboarding. Its San Francisco-based operations have supported deployments with major agricultural producers, including almond giant Campos Brothers Farms and the Duckhorn wineries. Along with its validation and R&D work, the raise allows Tellia to leverage its strong early US traction to pursue similar results in Europe, which has already seen Tellia deployed with institutions like the Institut Français de la Vigne et du Vin (IFV), cooperatives such as Val de Gascogne, or German plant breeder KWS Saat. “The Ag industry keeps facing the same challenge: the people who spend their days in the field spend their evenings at a keyboard,” said Coline Labadie de Faÿ, CEO and co-founder of Tellia. “That was never a data problem. It was an interface problem. Traditional software cannot accept it the way it actually comes out, spoken, in the field, in whatever language the team works in. So we did not build another platform that wants to own all the data. Instead, we built the interface. You talk, Tellia captures it, structures it, and interprets it into something the whole operation can act on. This funding round lets us push the voice AI further, build the agentic layer that sits between the field and the rest of the agtech stack, and grow our team in the US and Europe.” Every agtech platform runs into the same wall – data capture friction – so the field never makes it into the software. The funding will accelerate the rollout of Tellia’s agentic AI suite, built to close that gap. Partners embed it through a simple API: their users just talk, and Tellia captures, structures and interprets the field, delivering records and recommendations directly inside the partner’s own product. Richer data, higher daily usage, a new revenue stream, no rebuild. The first agritech partners are integrating it now. Revent’s general partner, Otto Birnbaum commented: “We believe that the voice first approach will lead the agricultural sector into the new agentic data age and that Tellia will be the category defining company here. Tellia is creating the critical data layer to meaningfully improve efficiencies and productivity in the agricultural sector. We are thrilled to partner with Coline and Vincent and are deeply impressed by their operational pace and how fast the product gets adopted on both sides of the Atlantic.” The round brings together an international syndicate with deep agriculture and technology expertise, spanning Europe and the US. For Tellia’s founders this investor base, which mirrors the diversity of their 13-strong team, is a signal of both credibility and global ambition. Tellia’s founders met through Entrepreneur First, the talent investor whose programme took them from Paris to San Francisco, where the company launched. Now operating on both sides of the Atlantic, Tellia combines US commercial traction with European standards around data protection, security and confidentiality, an important reassurance for agricultural businesses handling sensitive operational data. Its long-term ambition is to become the leading voice interface between agriculture and the technology that supports it.

title: Regeno’s AI-powered platform aims to simplify farm assurance and compliance
content: Spun out of Founders Factory and Nesta's venture builder programme, UK-based Regeno has pivoted from helping small farms access subsidies to tackling the...
raw_content: It’s easy for farmers to get lost in the ever-growing maze of subsidy rules, farm assurance schemes, and sustainability requirements. That’s exactly why Regeno was created. Spun out of Founders Factory and Nesta’s venture builder programme just over a year ago, the company has evolved from its original mission of helping small and medium-sized farms access government support to tackling the broader challenge of compliance and record-keeping across the agricultural sector. ATN sat down with CEO and co-founder Sven Poppelman to discuss the company’s early pivot and how its AI-driven approach is reshaping what farm assurance could look like. ATN: What’s the idea behind Regeno? We started as a way of lowering the bar for small and medium-sized farmers to access farming subsidies. So there was the SFI [UK government] scheme that got shut down in March. That then shut down our original business, which was using tech to find the right stack of funding options for farms. We went through a couple of pivots, and the main line now is farm assurance and record-keeping to help farmers implement the actions needed for assurance schemes. We’re interested in lowering the friction and making it really clear how to be accountable to the different schemes that you might be in as a food grower or producer. ATN: How does a farmer work with you? It’s a tech product they sign up to. They onboard the shape of their farm and then upload their agreements and basically overlay the set of actions onto that farm map. ATN: Why do they need it? The value for the farmer is lowering the risk of losing their subsidy. But the bit we’ve found real traction on is with consultants and land agents who have responsibility for getting farms into those sustainability assurance schemes and making sure they stay compliant. A consultant could be managing anywhere from 30 to 100 properties, and so trying to stay on top of all the different scheme requirements for all your different farms is either an exercise in being really good at Excel or having a photographic memory. ATN: So your customers are typically consultants rather than farmers? Yes, because we’ve lowered the friction on collecting evidence as well as filing and reporting the evidence. That’s been massive for consultants. The other area we are finding interest in is buyers, as a system of record for their partners. So for some barley growers in Scotland, for example, this is a great way for them to be accountable for their practices and to prove sustainability practices like cover cropping. ATN: What does the farmer need to do themselves to feed into the system? If they pull up their farm on the system, they see their parcels [of land] and if there’s any work to be done linked to any schemes. So, for example, in one field there might be 10 actions and 15 pieces of evidence to submit. So rather than reading a really dense and horrible PDF file with codes and dates and areas, we can tell them what the evidence requirements are for each. What is pretty unique is if you have something like a soil test report, uploading one test will satisfy the requirements for multiple agreements or schemes. ATN: Is there IP behind any of this? What stops someone coming along and programming the same system? Our advantage is we’ve heavily used AI to lower the friction beyond digital paperwork and record-keeping solutions. Most importantly, we’ve used AI to map unstructured data like conversations and videos into structured data. A farming consultant or farmer, for example, could record themselves talking about a hedgerow and turn that into a structured hedgerow survey. No one else has done that yet. We’ve been able to build all of this in a short space of time because my tech lead is basically the tech equivalent of God. He’s incredible, and I try not to let him cross the road without at least five people protecting him. ATN: Just in the UK? Yes, although there are schemes everywhere that require documentation and evidence, so there’s nothing limiting us from being international. ATN: Is the government and the schemes happy with it being done this way? At the end of the day, we’re not circumventing any existing systems. The information still needs to be submitted by the farmer using the official channels. We sat down with the RPA [Rural Payments Agency – the UK’s farming subsidies body] with an early product, and they had to go away and think about what it means because they’d never actually thought someone would come along and do compliance in this way. ATN: And you’re currently raising? Yes, I’m looking to raise and really pour fuel onto this fire because we’ve got some traction, we’ve got validation that people are willing to pay for it, and we’ve got the direction of travel that’s really set. So finding like-minded investors, some farmer investors, and a few more institutional investors, although it might be a little bit too early for us to be there.
